text: I'll start by looking at the workspace layout and searching for CSV-related code.
The root cause is clear: line 18 of `library/csv_import.py` forces the input through an ASCII encode with `errors="ignore"`, which silently drops every non-ASCII character. The test run confirms it.

args.root_cause: In parse_orders_csv, the first line of the function unconditionally coerces the entire CSV text to ASCII: `text = text.encode("ascii", errors="ignore").decode("ascii")`. Encoding to ASCII with errors="ignore" silently drops every non-ASCII code point before csv.DictReader ever sees the data, so accented letters vanish ("José Martínez" -> "Jos Martnez", "Åse" -> "se"). This is not a decoding/encoding mismatch in the reader itself; it is an explicit lossy ASCII filter applied to the whole input. The fix is to remove that line (the input is already a Python str, so no byte-level conversion is needed) and let the csv module handle Unicode text directly; if the source file is read from bytes, decode it as UTF-8 at the file-read boundary instead.

Non-blocking note: parse_orders_csv takes a str, so any caller reading raw bytes from a file must decode as UTF-8 at the read boundary (e.g. open with encoding='utf-8'). That is outside this diff; it is worth confirming in the real CSV import path that the file is decoded as UTF-8 rather than a legacy encoding such as cp1252, since a mismatch there would still garble names.
